analysis.one_liner: Strips the federal labor board of its power to prosecute employers and order remedies for unfair labor practices.
analysis.headline: The bill to strip the National Labor Relations Board of its enforcement powers was introduced in March 2021, referred to committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The National Labor Relations Board enforces federal labor law: it investigates charges, prosecutes employers accused of firing or punishing workers for organizing, issues orders to fix violations, and asks courts to enforce them. This bill would have removed nearly all of that. The board could only investigate and write a summary of findings; workers alleging violations would have to sue employers themselves in federal court; and the board could write rules only about its own internal operations, not about workers' or employers' rights. The bill never advanced past its committee assignment and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, employers would have gained the most. They would no longer face NLRB complaints, prosecutions, remedial orders, or court enforcement actions for alleged unfair labor practices such as firing workers for union activity; the only route to a remedy would have been an individual worker's lawsuit in federal court. The board's rulemaking would have been confined to its internal functions, rolling back regulations on topics like representation elections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers facing union organizing and NLRB complaints

how_it_helps.text: Employers would no longer face NLRB complaints, hearings, or remedial orders for alleged unfair labor practices; instead, a worker alleging a violation would have to file a civil lawsuit in federal court.

The Board could no longer write rules on unfair labor practices or representation elections, only on its own internal functions, and would have to review and revise or rescind existing regulations within six months.
The General Counsel would lose the power to prosecute complaints, and the Board could only investigate allegations and summarize findings, ending its role as prosecutor and judge in labor disputes.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would have borne the cost. Instead of a free federal agency investigating and prosecuting on their behalf, each worker alleging an illegal firing or anti-union retaliation would have to bring and finance a federal lawsuit against their employer, and the board could no longer order company-wide remedies or seek injunctions to stop ongoing violations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers relying on federal labor law enforcement

drawbacks.text: The bill would have replaced the NLRB's free complaint-and-order process with private lawsuits in federal court, shifting the cost and burden of enforcing labor law onto individual workers, who typically cannot match an employer's legal resources.

Without Board remedial orders, court enforcement petitions, or the ability to seek injunctions, remedies for illegal firings or union-busting would have come only after a worker won a lawsuit, a process that can take years.

The bill would have barred the Board from issuing any rule affecting the substantive rights of employers, employees, or unions, leaving contested questions of labor law to be settled only through individual litigation rather than uniform national rules — the strongest good-faith objection from supporters, who argued an unelected board had accumulated too much power to rewrite labor law by regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On paper, the bill's stated aim — reining in an agency that can write sweeping rules and prosecute employers without a jury — is a real policy debate, and the civil-action route would have preserved some remedy for workers. But the design put the full burden of enforcing federal labor law on individual employees, who rarely have the money to sue a corporation in federal court, while removing the agency's ability to order company-wide fixes or win quick injunctions against illegal firings. On balance the drawbacks were serious: enforcement of existing union and organizing rights would have weakened considerably.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee after being referred there, and no markup or vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 18, 2021 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — for the remainder of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.
The bill's congressional page shows no disposition beyond committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions, because the National Labor Relations Board kept its full authority to prosecute unfair labor practices, issue remedial orders, and enforce them in court. Employers who would have benefited from weaker enforcement gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers and unions, who kept NLRB enforcement

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bobby Scott, D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; it stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters — the sponsor and seven cosponsors — were Republicans, and the bill sat in a committee controlled by Democrats, who took no action on it; no vote was ever held.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those facing union organizing drives
industries.note: The bill would have removed the main federal mechanism that penalizes firing, threatening, or discriminating against workers for organizing, leaving enforcement to individual lawsuits most workers cannot afford. Employers accused of unfair labor practices would face investigation only, with no Board order against them.

Union organizing and bargaining depend heavily on NLRB elections, complaint prosecution, and enforcement orders, all of which the bill would have curtailed. Weaker enforcement makes it easier for employers to resist organizing without penalty.

industries.industry: National Labor Relations Board (as an institution)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the agency of its power to issue complaints, order remedies, write substantive rules, or ask courts to enforce its decisions, reducing it to an investigative body that writes summaries of findings.
